new_statements.quote: Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. That is, feet are left headed and quantity insensitive.
new_statements.citation: Boerger, Brenda H. 2022. A Grammar Sketch of Natqgu [ntu]: An Oceanic language of Santa Cruz, Solomon Islands. Port Moresby: Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea (LLM 'Texts in the Indigenous Languages of the Pacific' 2020-2023 collection). 71 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 4 (printed page 4; PDF page 5 area, between page footers 3 and 4); supporting example §2.5 Rule 4, p. 7
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: the full passage is present verbatim in the text layer of ( lines 177-183, heading "2.3 Stress"): "Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. That is, feet are left headed and quantity insensitive." Only the locator is slightly off: per-page extracted text shows page footers equal PDF page numbers,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (the author writes 'penultimate mora of a syllable', evidently meaning of the word) and stays penultimate in morphologically complex words; feet are left-headed, quantity-insensitive syllabic trochees, so secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables leftward. Stress is assigned before fast-speech deletion of word-final q [y], so a surface form such as [vztrpʰ] 'come in' can sound final-stressed (p. 7).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated in principle only: secondary stress follows the syllabic-trochee foot type (left-headed, quantity-insensitive); no examples given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as lexical exceptions. §2.1 (p. 3): a second vowel of a VV sequence that must bear stress is syllabified separately (na-iklö [na.'i.kʰlö]); §2.5 Rule 4 (p. 7): apparent surface final stress after word-final q-deletion. Older Wurm 1969: 60 / 1970: 477 / 1976: 643 n. 6 said stress only partly predictable and 'may be phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single morphemes and multisyllabic complex words, i.e. the verb complex); no phrase-level statement; impressionistic, no instrumental data; Natügu of the Graciosa Bay area (Bznwz village).
new_statements.identity_note: natu1249 is not a language: it is Glottolog's Bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [stc] "Santa Cruz", split on 2009-01-16 (CR 2008-070, into Natügu [ntu] = natu1246 (Northern Santa Cruz, Wurm's 'Malo') and Nalögo [nlz] = nalo1235 (Southern Santa Cruz). The statement quoted is the Natügu one (natu1246), which already has a WORLD_RESULTS entry with this same quote; Nalögo's stress is described separately by Alfarano 2021 §2.5 (weight-sensitive, mora-based) in the nalo1235 catalog folder. Recommend reclassification natu1249 -> natu1246 (with nalo1235 as the second referent) rather than cataloguing it as its own row.

sources.quote: Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. sources.locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 4 (printed page 4; PDF page 5 area, between page footers 3 and 4); supporting example §2.5 Rule 4, p. 7
sources.note: §2.3 Stress, p. 4: stress on the penultimate mora ('of a syllable' sic, i.e. of the word); primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words; secondary stress follows the foot type, a left-headed quantity-insensitive syllabic trochee. §2.5 Rule 4, p. 7: penultimate stress is assigned before word-final q-deletion, so vz-tr-mq 'come in' -> [vztrpʰ] keeps stress on trpʰ.

sources.citation: Alfarano, Valentina. 2021. A grammar of Nalögo, an Oceanic language of Santa Cruz Island. PhD thesis, INALCO, Paris (HAL tel-03421587).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §2.5 Stress assignment, pp. 87-90 (analysis 'very preliminary'): mora-sensitive; disyllables of two light syllables stressed on the first (/ˈna.wɜ/ 'head'), light+heavy on the heavy final (/nɒ.ˈdɵk/ 'wall', /to.ˈkoi/ 'tongs'); most trisyllables penultimate (/be.ˈte.pu/), some initial (/ˈtɵ.pu.ti/ 'cat'); affixes and clitics count for stress, prefix i- extrametrical, a heavy suffix attracts stress (/i.ˈpwɵk/). Covers the other half of the retired [stc] scope (Nalögo = S. Santa Cruz).
